court: N.Y. Court of Appeals, Second Division
notes: Copartnership accounting dispute over destruction of contributed factory property by fire and risk-of-loss doctrine; no bearing on letting of dwellings or lodging houses.

holding_summary: Plaintiff sued a boarding-house/innkeeper for loss of goods on a bailment theory; defendant answered that he had agreed to furnish plaintiff board and lodging in his boarding-house at $30/week for over seven months, and counterclaimed the unpaid balance. The court held the counterclaim proper under Code section 150 because it arose out of the same contract of bailment, treating the board-and-lodging arrangement as an ordinary enforceable contract.

quotes.text: defendant was to furnish plaintiff with board and lodging in defendant’s boarding-house, for thirty dollars a week, in pursuance of which he was received and boarded upwards of seven months.

This action is not one of tort brought for the conversion of goods, but it is brought for a cause of action arising out of a contract of bailment between the parties, and is to recover damages for the breach of that contract by the defendant.
The defendant seeks to counter-claim a cause of action arising to him out of the self same contract.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
notes: Statutory-conflict case about board of health authority to regulate petroleum/kerosene storage and sale; no connection to lodging or letting of dwellings.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
notes: Non-residence/attachment motion turning on where defendant maintained his 'home'; defendant's own furnished apartment above his store is discussed only to determine his domicile, not as a letting to another occupant.
Commercial lease covenant dispute over liability for a street repaving assessment; no bearing on lodging/boarding practice.

court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Defendant operated a bathing house whose upper floors were let in apartments to lodgers, including plaintiff. The court held that a lodging-house keeper does not assume bailee responsibility for a lodger's goods absent custody, and that even under a duty of ordinary care, plaintiff's own negligence in leaving his room unlocked barred recovery for clothing stolen from his room.

quotes.text: The defendant kept a bathing house, the upper floors of which were let in apartments to lodgers.
There is authority for holding that a lodging house keeper like the defendant does not assume responsibility for the goods of his lodger, as he does not take them into his custody.

But conceding that the defendant was bound, as a lodging house keeper, to take the same care of the plaintiff’s property that a prudent person takes of his own, the defendant, nevertheless, was entitled to judgment in his favor.

Divorce action; 'boarding-house keeper and boarder' invoked only as a rhetorical comparison for the intimacy of the parties' relations, a passing mention with no ruling on lodging/boarding law.

court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: In an execution-exemption dispute, the court held plaintiff was not a 'householder' entitled to statutory exemptions because, after his wife's death, he had no family or household, even in his own house; in reaching this the court noted, citing precedent, that a person living in a hired house who keeps servants and boarders is properly deemed a householder.

quotes.text: And it has been held that a person living in a hired house and keeping servants and boarders is a householder.

The difficulty in the defense of the case at bar is that. while the plaintiff had a house in which he resided, he had no family or persons there or elsewhere for whom he provided or who constituted a household; he, therefore, came within neither alternative.

notes: Characterization left null: the case does not classify the letting arrangement itself (lease/license/lodging); the boarder-householder point is cited doctrine, not a fact at issue for this plaintiff, who kept no boarders.
